topic.title: Index laws in algebra for fractional and negative powers
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: Both M8 papers, most series, for 2 or 3 marks. On Paper 2 it is an early question of three one-mark index statements with a blank index (Summer 2025 Q3, where about three candidates in four answered every part correctly; November 2025 Q2, two one-mark simplifications which the report describes as confidently done). On Paper 1 it sits around Q8 to Q11 for 2 or 3 marks, usually a bracket with a coefficient raised to an outside power (November 2025 Q11(a); November 2024 Q8; Summer 2024 Q10, 3 marks).
mustMemorise: a^m x a^n = a^(m+n), a^m / a^n = a^(m-n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn) — unchanged for fractional and negative indices
The indices themselves are added, subtracted and multiplied as ordinary fractions and directed numbers
A power outside a bracket acts on the coefficient as well as on every letter inside
Numbers in front are multiplied or divided normally; only the indices are added or subtracted
Rewrite every root as a fractional power before using any law: the nth root of x^m is x^(m/n)
The answer must be a single term, with no times sign left in it
notOnThisSpec: Logarithms, so an index equation is solved by matching bases rather than by taking logs
Simplifying surd expressions for their own sake, which is M8-NA-01 and a separate topic here
Negative or fractional indices applied to a sum, such as (x + y)^(1/2), which no index law simplifies

note.title: Index laws in algebra: fractional and negative powers
note.subject: maths

given: Nothing: the Higher formula sheet carries no index law
mustKnow: A bracket power acts on the coefficient as well as on the letters
The nth root of x^m is x^(m/n), so every root can be rewritten as a power

notOnThisSpec: Applying an index law to a sum, such as (x + y)^(1/2)

mustBeAbleTo: Add, subtract and multiply fractional and negative indices when terms are multiplied, divided or raised to a power
Raise a bracket containing a coefficient to an integer or fractional power, rooting or powering the number as well
Rewrite a root as a fractional index before applying any law
Combine a negative index with a negative outside index, so that two minus signs multiply to a plus
Fill in a missing index in a printed statement, the Paper 2 shape
Write the answer as a single term with no times sign, and say whether a negative index or a fraction is wanted
Use an earlier part's simplified term in a later part, so the follow-through the scheme allows is available
sheet.howExamined: Both M8 papers. Paper 2 often opens with index statements to complete or simplify, one mark each (Summer 2025 Q3, three blanks, all three right for about three candidates in four; November 2025 Q2, which the report calls confidently done). Paper 1 carries a 2 or 3 mark simplification around Q8 to Q11, usually a bracket with a number in front: schemes give A2 for the single term and A1 for two of its three parts right (November 2025 Q11(a); November 2024 Q8), or a bracket power then a division for 3 marks (Summer 2024 Q10, full marks for just over a quarter).
traps: Two of the three parts of a bracket answer right, the number or one letter's index wrong: one mark of two (November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q11(a))
Multiplying the indices when the terms are multiplied (November 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q8)
Leaving a times sign in the final answer, so it is not a single term (November 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q8)
Going wrong on the power of a power when the simpler laws were right (Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q3)
Leaving the number in front untouched inside a bracket power, or multiplying it by the outside index
Adding fractional indices by adding numerators and denominators separately
Leaving a root sign in place, so the laws cannot be applied
Dropping the minus sign on an index, so a subtraction that should add takes away instead

noteBlocks.lede: The index laws you already know keep working when an index is a fraction or negative: multiplying adds the indices, dividing subtracts them, a power of a power multiplies them. The new skill is that arithmetic with fractions and minus signs, and remembering the number in front.
can: Add, subtract and multiply fractional and negative indices.
Raise a bracket with a number in front to any power.
Rewrite a root as a power before using a law.

noteBlocks.md: An index tells you how many times a base is used as a factor. With fractions and minus signs there is nothing to count, but the three laws were extended so that they still hold, so you can trust them and do ordinary arithmetic on the indices.

noteBlocks.caption: The indices are just numbers: add for multiplying, subtract for dividing.

noteBlocks.md: $x^{a} \times x^{b} = x^{a+b}$ and $x^{a} \div x^{b} = x^{a-b}$: multiplying adds the indices and dividing subtracts them. That is true whatever kind of number the indices are, so the only new work is the arithmetic. Add fractions as fractions, thirds with thirds, and take care with a minus sign: subtracting a negative index adds.

steps.decision: Multiplying adds the indices; thirds add to thirds.
Dividing subtracts the index, and subtracting $-2$ adds 2.
One term, one index.

That multiplies the indices; multiplying the terms adds them.

noteBlocks.md: Each step down the bars takes 1 off the index and halves the value. Carry on past $2^{0} = 1$ and the index goes negative: $2^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}$, $2^{-2} = \frac{1}{4}$. So $x^{-n} = \frac{1}{x^{n}}$. That is why a division whose bottom power is bigger gives a negative index, and why the laws still hold below zero.

noteBlocks.title: Why a negative index is one over
noteBlocks.md: Dividing $x^{3}$ by $x^{3}$ gives 1 because anything divided by itself is 1, and the law gives $x^{0}$, so $x^{0} = 1$. Divide once more by $x$ and the law gives $x^{-1}$ while the value is $\frac{1}{x}$. The law and the arithmetic agree only if $x^{-1} = \frac{1}{x}$.

noteBlocks.stem: Simplify $d^{3} \div d^{8}$, then write the answer as a fraction.

steps.decision: Dividing subtracts; the bigger power is underneath, so the index goes below zero.
A negative index means one over the positive power.

noteBlocks.explain: Multiplying adds the indices, minus signs and all: $-4 + (-3) = -7$, as step 1 of See it keeps the sign of each index.

twin.explain: Dividing subtracts, and the index taken away is negative: $2 - (-6) = 8$. Subtracting a negative adds, as step 2 of the first See it shows.

optionNotes.why: That works 2 − 6; the index taken away is −6, and 2 − (−6) is 8.
That divides the indices; dividing the terms subtracts them.
That subtracts the wrong way round, −6 − 2; take the bottom index from the top one.
That multiplies the indices; multiplying the terms adds them.
One minus sign was lost: −4 plus −3 is −7, not −1.
Both minus signs were dropped; adding two negatives stays negative.

noteBlocks.text: A power of a power multiplies

noteBlocks.md: $\left(x^{a}\right)^{b} = x^{ab}$: a power of a power multiplies the indices, so a fraction or a minus sign outside the bracket multiplies the index inside. Two minus signs multiplied give a plus, and a fraction usually cancels with the index it meets.

steps.decision: Multiply the indices; the 4 cancels with the 8.
Two negatives multiply to a positive.

noteBlocks.explain: A power of a power multiplies the indices, as step 1 of See it does: $10 \times \frac{3}{5} = 6$.

twin.explain: Multiply the indices, keeping the sign, as in See it: $-6 \times \frac{2}{3} = -4$.

optionNotes.why: The minus sign on −6 was dropped; −6 times two thirds is −4.
That adds the indices; a power of a power multiplies them.
That multiplies by the fraction upside down: the 3 is the root, the 2 the power.
That adds the two indices; a power of a power multiplies them.
That multiplies by the fraction upside down: the 5 is the root, the 3 the power.
That applies only the fifth root and forgets to cube.

noteBlocks.md: A power outside a bracket acts on everything inside, the number included: the cube of edge $2a$ holds eight small cubes, so $(2a)^{3} = 8a^{3}$, not $2a^{3}$. Deal with the number on its own (power it, or root it), then multiply each letter's index. Numbers in front are never added to indices.

noteBlocks.explain: As in step 1 of See it, the number is cubed too: $4^{3} = 64$. Then $3 \times 3 = 9$ and $-2 \times 3 = -6$, giving $64x^{9}y^{-6}$.

twin.explain: The number is raised as well, step 1 of See it: $2^{4} = 16$. Then $-1 \times 4 = -4$ and $5 \times 4 = 20$.

That multiplies the 2 by 4; raised to the power 4 it is 16.
The number is right, but the indices were added to 4; a power of a power multiplies them.
The indices are right but the 4 was left alone; the bracket power cubes it too.
That multiplies the 4 by 3; the 4 is cubed, 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.

noteBlocks.md: An index of $\frac{1}{2}$ is a square root and $\frac{1}{3}$ a cube root: the square's side times itself makes its area. In $\frac{2}{3}$ the bottom number is the root and the top the power. So a fractional power on a bracket roots the number in front, then powers it, while each letter's index is multiplied by the fraction as before.

steps.decision: Cube root first (the 3 underneath), then square (the 2 on top).
Each letter's index is multiplied by two thirds.
One term: the number, then the letters.

noteBlocks.explain: As in step 1 of See it, the number is rooted: the fourth root of 81 is 3. Each index is multiplied by a quarter: $8 \div 4 = 2$ and $-12 \div 4 = -3$.

twin.explain: The cube root reaches the number, step 1 of See it: $\sqrt[3]{125} = 5$. Each index is divided by 3: $-6 \div 3 = -2$, $9 \div 3 = 3$.

optionNotes.why: The indices are right but the 125 was left alone; the cube root reaches it too.
That divides 125 by 3; a power of one third takes the cube root, 5.
That multiplies the indices by 3; a power of one third divides them by 3.
The indices are right but the 81 was left alone; the quarter power roots it too.
That divides 81 by 4; a power of one quarter takes the fourth root, 3.
That multiplies the indices by 4; a power of one quarter divides them by 4.

noteBlocks.md: The laws work on powers only, so translate every root before combining: $\sqrt{x} = x^{\frac{1}{2}}$, $\sqrt[3]{x} = x^{\frac{1}{3}}$, and the $n$th root of $x^{m}$ is $x^{\frac{m}{n}}$, the root underneath and the power on top. After that the question is ordinary index arithmetic with fractions.

noteBlocks.stem: Simplify $\sqrt{z} \times \sqrt[3]{z}$, giving your answer as a power of $z$.

steps.decision: Translate both roots into powers before using a law.
Multiplying adds the indices: a common denominator first.
One power of $z$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt{t^{7}} \div t^{2}$, giving your answer as a power of $t$.
noteBlocks.explain: Translate first, as step 1 of See it does: $\sqrt{t^{7}} = t^{\frac{7}{2}}$. Dividing subtracts: $\frac{7}{2} - 2 = \frac{3}{2}$.

twin.prompt: Simplify $\sqrt[3]{s^{4}} \times s^{\frac{2}{3}}$, giving your answer as a power of $s$.
twin.explain: Translate first, step 1 of See it: $\sqrt[3]{s^{4}} = s^{\frac{4}{3}}$. Multiplying adds: $\frac{4}{3} + \frac{2}{3} = 2$.

optionNotes.why: The root was ignored: 4 + 2 treats the cube root of s⁴ as s⁴.
That multiplies the indices; multiplying the terms adds them.
That adds the tops and the bottoms separately, six sixths; four thirds plus two thirds is six thirds, 2.
The root was ignored: 7 − 2 treats the square root of t⁷ as t⁷.
That divides the indices; dividing the terms subtracts them.
That adds the indices, the rule for multiplying; this is a division.

noteBlocks.md: **A blank index.** Paper 2 often opens with statements to complete, a missing index in each (Summer 2025 Paper 2 Q3; November 2025 Paper 2 Q2). Write the law as an equation in the blank and solve it.
**A division as a fraction.** $\dfrac{w^{9}}{w^{4}}$ is $w^{9} \div w^{4}$: subtract (November 2025 Paper 2 Q2).
**A bracket power, then a division.** Raise the bracket first, number included, then divide numbers as numbers and subtract indices (Summer 2024 Paper 1 Q10).
**One term.** $6a^{3}b$, never $6 \times a^{3}b$: a times sign left in loses the mark (November 2024 Paper 1 Q8).

steps.decision: Multiplying adds the indices, so write that as an equation.
Solve for the blank.
Put it back into the law.

noteBlocks.prompt: Complete: $k^{\square} \times k^{-2} = k^{\frac{1}{3}}$. What is the missing index?
noteBlocks.explain: Write the law as an equation, as in step 1 of See it: $\square + (-2) = \frac{1}{3}$, so $\square = \frac{1}{3} + 2 = \frac{7}{3}$.

twin.prompt: Complete: $\left(m^{\square}\right)^{4} = m^{-6}$. What is the missing index?
twin.explain: A power of a power multiplies, so $\square \times 4 = -6$ and $\square = -6 \div 4 = -\frac{3}{2}$. Solve for the blank, as step 2 of See it does.

optionNotes.why: That takes 4 from −6; a power of a power multiplies, so divide −6 by 4.
That multiplies −6 by 4; the blank times 4 is −6, so divide instead.
The minus sign was dropped: −6 divided by 4 is negative.
That takes 2 away from one third; the blank plus −2 makes one third, so the blank is 2 more.
That multiplies one third by −2; multiplying the terms adds the indices.
That divides one third by −2; the indices are added, so subtract −2 from one third.

noteBlocks.md:
Add indices when multiplying and subtract them when dividing, with fractions and minus signs.
Multiply indices for a power of a power.
Raise or root the number in front with every letter in a bracket.
Rewrite a root as a power before using any law.

Usually an early Paper 2 question of one-mark blanks, or a 2 to 3 mark 'Simplify' on Paper 1 with a bracket and a number in front. Two of three parts right in a bracket answer keeps one mark; the last mark needs all of it as one term. Stuck: do the number, then each letter, on separate lines.

workedExamples.stem:
Simplify $\left(2a^{3}b^{-2}\right)^{4} \div 4b^{-3}$.

Give your answer as a single term.

steps.decision: The power outside the bracket lands on everything inside, the $2$ included: $2^{4} = 16$, and each index inside is multiplied by $4$. Leaving the number untouched is the single commonest slip on this question type.

options: Because a bracket power multiplies every index inside and raises the coefficient too
Because the coefficient stays outside brackets and is never affected
Because the indices inside a bracket are added to the outside power

prompts.answer: It rises, because subtracting a negative adds.
